query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a thin, dense ceramic nitride coating (approximately 5–10 µm) on boride-based substrates via a controlled high-temperature CVD or plasma-assisted method will form an aluminum-impermeable barrier that significantly slows molten-aluminum attack, thereby improving corrosion resistance relative to uncoated boride components in hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Uncoated boride-based components intended for use in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment
generation.intervention: Apply a 5–10 µm thick ceramic nitride coating (e.g., TiN or ZrN) using a high-temperature CVD or plasma-based surface engineering process to ensure a dense, well-adhered protective layer
generation.conditions: Continuous exposure to molten aluminum at typical hot-dip plating temperatures (~700–750 °C) over multiple thermal cycles
generation.structural_mediator: A stable nitride-based barrier film that reduces direct contact between molten aluminum and the boride substrate
generation.mechanism: The ceramic nitride layer hinders aluminum infiltration and minimizes reactive diffusion, preventing the rapid degradation of borides by oxidation/dissolution reactions in molten aluminum
generation.predicted_outcome: A substantial reduction in corrosion-related mass loss and surface damage relative to uncoated boride components, with an expected extension of service life by at least a factor of two
generation.baseline: Corrosion rates and component lifetimes of boride-based substrates without a protective coating under the same operating conditions
generation.boundary: Maintains effectiveness under steady temperatures and moderate thermal cycling; severe mechanical damage or unexpected chemical contamination may compromise the protective layer’s integrity and reduce benefit
generation.uncertainty: Long-term durability in actual production environments and the precise quantitative improvement in corrosion resistance are not fully characterized, pending expanded testing and field trials

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based coupons—one with the nitride coating (5–10 µm) and one uncoated—and immerse them in a molten-aluminum bath at 725 °C for fixed intervals (e.g., 100, 200, 300 hours). Assess coating integrity, mass change, depth of aluminum diffusion, and microstructural degradation via SEM/EDS after each interval.
measurements: Mass change in each coupon to assess cumulative material loss
Depth of aluminum penetration, evaluated by cross-sectional microstructural examination
Microhardness profiles across the coating and substrate interface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If coated samples exhibit a mass loss, infiltration depth, or microstructural damage statistically indistinguishable from uncoated controls, this would falsify the hypothesis that the nitride coating provides improved molten-aluminum corrosion resistance.

The microstructure, microhardness, wear resistance, and boriding mechanism were investigated. The following conclusions can be summarized: The microstructure of the surface layer is mainly composed of MB-type boride and M2B-type boride. The original interface of the surface layer is located at the interface between the BL and the diffusion layer, where element B diffuses inward and metal elements diffuse outward. The activation energy and frequency factor of the B element in CoCrFeMnNi HEA are 206.93 kJ/mol and 9.15 × 10−5 m2/s, respectively. Increasing the boronizing duration and temperature resulted in an increase in the BL and diffusion layer thickness. The surface strengthening of CoCrFeMnNi HEA was achieved by the boriding treatment. Its surface microhardness has significantly increased from 3.9 ± 0.1 Gpa to 23.8 ± 1.4 Gpa. The surface layer shows a lower friction coefficient of 0.48 than that of the substrate (0.86). decision.trend: Although no prior work in these references deals specifically with boride-based alloys in molten aluminum, two studies have tangential relevance for high-temperature corrosion control through surface engineering. In PMC7240591, short atmospheric-pressure plasma treatments created protective oxide layers that significantly improved corrosion resistance in a medium-entropy alloy. In PMC10488378, laser-cladded high-entropy alloy coatings enhanced hot-corrosion performance in molten salt at elevated temperatures. Together, these works suggest that building a stable, protective surface layer—whether by plasma-induced passivation or by applying a specialized coating—can be an effective means to shield metals from aggressive molten environments. However, none of the studies addresses the challenge of molten-aluminum corrosion in boride-based components directly, leaving open the question of how best to engineer a robust, adherent coating that survives prolonged contact with molten aluminum at typical hot-dip process temperatures (≈700–750 °C).
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear which protective interface coatings can best accommodate thermal and chemical stresses while resisting molten aluminum attack on boride-based substrates. Data are lacking on the interplay between molten-aluminum infiltration and the stability of potential barrier layers over many cycles of thermal and chemical exposure. Furthermore, the optimal processing route (e.g., plasma enhancement, diffusion barriers, or advanced cladding) for reliable, scalable manufacturing has not been established.
decision.lever: Deposit a thin, dense, aluminum-impermeable coating (e.g., a ceramic nitride or oxide) via a controlled high-temperature chemical vapor deposition (CVD) or plasma-assisted process to form a stable barrier on boride-based substrates. Target ~5–10 µm thickness with strong interfacial adhesion, ensuring minimal diffusion pathways.
decision.why: Building on trends showing that engineered surface modifications can impede corrosive ingress in high-temperature molten environments, applying a well-bonded, oxidation-resistant coating to boride-based alloys is a logical next step. A CVD or plasma-generated ceramic barrier can foreclose direct molten-aluminum contact, slow detrimental diffusion, and reduce chemical attack at the boride interface—thereby offering improved corrosion resistance and longer service life in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
